div.head:
[Translation]
To the Mischievously Idle Reader.
div.p: You, whoever you are, I declare: by all means watch you don’t rashly insult the author of this work, or be a quibbler and mock him. No, you shouldn’t secretly criticize him (to say it in a word) because of other people’s judgements, nor, like some little satirist, foolishly object or invent falsehoods. For if, in fact, Democritus Junior is what he says he is, is at least a relative of the elder Democritus, or if his own genius savours ever so slightly of him, then it’s all over for you: If somebody provokes me, I shout, ‘Better not touch!’ {Horace}he’ll turn on you as both judge and prosecutor (‘as he’s got a petulant spleen’), he’ll puff you up with jokes, crush you with wisecracks – and, I add, he’ll sacrifice you to the god of laughter.

Again, I warn you not to quibble lest, while you defame Democritus Junior with insults, or disparage him disgracefully (he feels no ill-will towards you), you should hear from a wise friend what the Abderitans once heard from I was summoned to cure Democritus, who was apparently insane; but when I met him, by god, I discovered his work wasn’t foolish, but was a storehouse of all truths, and I was astonished at his genius. Indeed, I accused the Abderitans of being just as insane, saying it was rather they that needed a dose of hellebore.Hippocrates, when they believed that their well-deserving fellow citizen and countryman Democritus was insane: ‘Really, it’s you, Democritus, who are wise, and the Abderitans who are fools and madmen.’

lg.l: You have the brains of the Abderitan plebs.

div.p: You’ve been warned with these few words; I mean, mischievously idle reader, begone!
